title: Finite Difference Methods for One Way Wave Equation
html:
1.1. A prototypical example: Euler method for an ODE

Already in the 18th century, Leonhard Euler had considered the problem of finding an approximation of the integral curve associated to an initial value problem of an ordinary differential equation. The solution to the initial value problem can be represented as a parametrised curve lying in the spatial domain: one can imagine it is a particle going along the curve, the position and velocity at certain time is defined by the differential equation and the initial position and velocity of the particle. More concretely, we may consider the first order ODE with an initial condition

dxdt(t)=f(t,x(t))x(0)=x0\displaystyle \frac{dx}{dt}(t)=f(t,x(t))\quad x(0)=x_{0}dtdx​(t)=f(t,x(t))x(0)=x0​

where, say, the solution lies in the plane x(t)∈R2 {x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}x(t)∈R2 for time interval t∈(0,1) {t\in(0,1)}t∈(0,1), and f:(0,1)×R2→R2 {f:(0,1)\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}}f:(0,1)×R2→R2. The famous Picard-Lindel{ö}f theorem asserts that if f {f}f is uniformly Lipschitz in the spatial variable x {x}x and continuous in the time variable y {y}y, then there exists a unique solution x(t) {x(t)}x(t) to the initial value problem. Of course, we don't expect to get closed form solution for every given right hand side satisfying the theorem. So, as Euler did, we want to try to directly integrate the differential equation by discrete approximation. The obvious thing to try is

x(ti)−x(ti−1)≈Δt⋅f(ti−1,x(ti−1)),(1) \displaystyle x(t_{i})-x(t_{i-1})\approx\Delta t\cdot f(t_{i-1},x(t_{i-1})), (1)x(ti​)−x(ti−1​)≈Δt⋅f(ti−1​,x(ti−1​)),(1)

where the time interval has been discretized 0=t0<t1<⋯<tn=1 {0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}=1}0=t0​<t1​<⋯<tn​=1 with equal distance Δt {\Delta t}Δt. Taking approximation

x~(ti)−x~(ti−1)=Δt⋅f(ti−1,x~(ti−1)),\displaystyle \tilde{x}(t_{i})-\tilde{x}(t_{i-1})=\Delta t\cdot f(t_{i-1},\tilde{x}(t_{i-1})),x~(ti​)−x~(ti−1​)=Δt⋅f(ti−1​,x~(ti−1​)),

we can then compute x~(ti) {\tilde{x}(t_{i})}x~(ti​) assuming x(ti−1) {x(t_{i-1})}x(ti−1​) is known. This is called Euler method. Since we are computing x~(ti) {\tilde{x}(t_{i})}x~(ti​) in terms of its values at previous times, we say it is an explicit method. In Riemann integration terms, we note that here we evaluate the integrand at the left endpoint in each subinterval. If evaluating at the right endpoint we arrive at an implicit method, called the backward Euler method, because now we have to solve a more difficult equation about x~(ti) {\tilde{x}(t_{i})}x~(ti​). It is of most interest to study the error produced by the discrete approximation. Inspecting more closely, we see that (1) is actually the first order Taylor approximation of x(ti) {x(t_{i})}x(ti​) based at ti−1 {t_{i-1}}ti−1​: if the solution x(t) {x(t)}x(t) is twice differentiable, by Taylor's theorem, we have an estimate

x(ti)=x(ti−1)+Δt⋅f(ti−1,x(ti−1))+O(Δt2)\displaystyle x(t_{i})=x(t_{i-1})+\Delta t\cdot f(t_{i-1},x(t_{i-1}))+O(\Delta t^{2})x(ti​)=x(ti−1​)+Δt⋅f(ti−1​,x(ti−1​))+O(Δt2)

where O(Δt2) {O(\Delta t^{2})}O(Δt2) is a quantity bounded by C⋅Δt2 {C\cdot\Delta t^{2}}C⋅Δt2 for some constant C {C}C and for all Δt {\Delta t}Δt small enough. Note that here we are using the true values of the solution. Rearranging and writing t=ti {t=t_{i}}t=ti​, Δt=h {\Delta t=h}Δt=h, dx/dt=f {dx/dt=f}dx/dt=f, the above estimate turns to

x(t+h)−x(t)h−dx(t)dt=O(h).\displaystyle \frac{x(t+h)-x(t)}{h}-\frac{dx(t)}{dt}=O(h).hx(t+h)−x(t)​−dtdx(t)​=O(h).

The difference in the LHS is known as the truncation error of the method. Since h {h}h is in its first power in the RHS O(h) {O(h)}O(h), we say that Euler method is of first order accurate. The above discussion holds when h {h}h is small enough. The behavior of Euler's method can be wild if h {h}h is sufficiently large. Indeed, consider the stiff problem:

dxdt(t)=−k⋅x(t),k>0\displaystyle \frac{dx}{dt}(t)=-k\cdot x(t),k>0dtdx​(t)=−k⋅x(t),k>0

This equation has solutions of the form x(t)=Ae−kt+C {x(t)=Ae^{-kt}+C}x(t)=Ae−kt+C. Clearly any particular solution decays to a fixed value as t→∞ {t\rightarrow\infty}t→∞, but one can check if the time step h≫1/k {h\gg1/k}h≫1/k, then the numerical solution will oscillate or even diverge to infinity. In some sense the solution is only stable (here, we mean continuous dependence on the initial condition with fixed step size) within a region of choice of h {h}h, or sometimes a expression in terms of h; we call a stability region the subset where the numerical solution for the stiff problem is stable. It turns out that here much of the analysis of a difference method (e.g. Euler's method) to solving the stiff problem is about the associated difference equation, which further breaks down to a linear algebraic problem of analysing eigenvalues of the associated linear system, recalling that the solution of a difference equation can be written as a linear combination of roots of the characteristic polynomial (though the case of multiple roots is slightly more complicated).

We shall see how these ideas in this case of Euler method correspond to those in the analysis of finite difference methods for hyperbolic PDEs, by examining the prototypical example, that of the one way wave equation with the initial condition

ut+aux=0u(0,x)=u0(x),\displaystyle u_{t}+au_{x}=0\quad u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),{} ut​+aux​=0u(0,x)=u0​(x),

where u:(0,T)×R→R {u:(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}u:(0,T)×R→R, and a {a}a is a constant. We note that if b,f=0 {b,f=0}b,f=0, the unique solution is given by

u(t,x)=u0(x−at),\displaystyle u(t,x)=u_{0}(x-at),u(t,x)=u0​(x−at),

as we see that the initial state is propogating at a constant speed in the direction (1,a) {(1,a)}(1,a). The homogeneous equations such as (⋆) {(\star)}(⋆) do not have issues of approximating the RHS. For sake of including a more comprehensive picture, we will also temporarily discuss the inhomogeneous case

ut+aux=fu(0,x)=u0(x),\displaystyle u_{t}+au_{x}=f\quad u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),ut​+aux​=fu(0,x)=u0​(x),

where f:(0,T)×R→R {f:(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}f:(0,T)×R→R is allowed to depend on both the time variable and spatial variable, but NOT u {u}u, otherwise it will be nonlinear. The closed form solution can be given by the method of variation of parameter:

u(t,x)=u0(x−at)+∫0tf(s,x−a(t−s))ds.\displaystyle u(t,x)=u_{0}(x-at)+\int_{0}^{t}f(s,x-a(t-s))ds.u(t,x)=u0​(x−at)+∫0t​f(s,x−a(t−s))ds.

We shall work with the initial value problem that is well-posed: if for any t∈(0,T) {t\in(0,T)}t∈(0,T), there is a constant CT {C_{T}}CT​ such that any solution u(t,x) {u(t,x)}u(t,x) will satisfy

∫−∞∞∣u(t,x)∣2dx≤CT∫−∞∞∣u(0,x)∣2dx.\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|u(t,x)|^{2}dx\leq C_{T}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|u(0,x)|^{2}dx.∫−∞∞​∣u(t,x)∣2dx≤CT​∫−∞∞​∣u(0,x)∣2dx.

It is important to note that in this post we don't consider nonlinear PDEs, as the analysis below in general does not apply.

1.2. Introduction to finite difference schemes

To do finite difference, we have to discretize the domain U=(0,T)×R {U=(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}}U=(0,T)×R by defining gird points (tn,xm)∈U {(t_{n},x_{m})\in U}(tn​,xm​)∈U, such that they form a rectanglular lattice. We denote h,k>0 {h,k>0}h,k>0 to be the spatial step and time step, respectively. The function u,f {u,f}u,f will thus be approximated by a function vmn,fmn {v_{m}^{n},f_{m}^{n}}vmn​,fmn​ defined on the grid points. Since f {f}f is given, we may simply take fmn {f_{m}^{n}}fmn​ to be f {f}f evaluated at the grid points. Similar is for vm0 {v_{m}^{0}}vm0​. We have to find a way to compute vnm {v_{n}^{m}}vnm​ such that it approximates u {u}u at the grid points. As before, we will try to integrate the PDE (⋆) {(\star)}(⋆). There are several ways to approximate its partial derivatives. Notably:
(Spatial) Forward Differece:

δ+vm=vm+1−vmh\displaystyle \delta_{+}v_{m}=\frac{v_{m+1}-v_{m}}{h}δ+​vm​=hvm+1​−vm​​

(Spatial) Backward Difference:

δ−vm=vm−vm−1h\displaystyle \delta_{-}v_{m}=\frac{v_{m}-v_{m-1}}{h}δ−​vm​=hvm​−vm−1​​

(Spatial) Central Difference:

δ0vm=vm+1−vm−12h\displaystyle \delta_{0}v_{m}=\frac{v_{m+1}-v_{m-1}}{2h}δ0​vm​=2hvm+1​−vm−1​​

Of course, the partial derivative in time variable can be approximated in the same way. Combining these approximations in some certain way that corresponds to the structure of (⋆) {(\star)}(⋆), we obtain a finite difference scheme. For instances, suppose f=0 {f=0}f=0:
Forward-time Central-space:

vmn+1−vmnk+avm+1n−vm−1n2h=0\displaystyle \frac{v_{m}^{n+1}-v_{m}^{n}}{k}+a\frac{v_{m+1}^{n}-v_{m-1}^{n}}{2h}=0kvmn+1​−vmn​​+a2hvm+1n​−vm−1n​​=0

Note that vmn+1 {v_{m}^{n+1}}vmn+1​ can be written as a linear combination of grid function evaluated at the n {n}n-th time level. Such a scheme will be called explicit, and the grid function is computed level after level.
Leap-frog:

vmn+1−vmn−12k+avm+1n−vm−1n2h=0\displaystyle \frac{v_{m}^{n+1}-v_{m}^{n-1}}{2k}+a\frac{v_{m+1}^{n}-v_{m-1}^{n}}{2h}=02kvmn+1​−vmn−1​​+a2hvm+1n​−vm−1n​​=0

Here we find that we cannot compute vmn+1 {v_{m}^{n+1}}vmn+1​ without knowing the previous two time levels vmn−1 {v_{m}^{n-1}}vmn−1​ and vm±1n {v_{m\pm1}^{n}}vm±1n​. Such will be called a multi-step scheme, and the initial condition has to specify the values of two time levels, or to get the second time level using some one-step scheme first.
Lax-Friedrichs:

vmn+1−12(vm+1n+vm−1n)k+avm+1n−vm−1n2h=0\displaystyle \frac{v_{m}^{n+1}-\frac{1}{2}(v_{m+1}^{n}+v_{m-1}^{n})}{k}+a\frac{v_{m+1}^{n}-v_{m-1}^{n}}{2h}=0kvmn+1​−21​(vm+1n​+vm−1n​)​+a2hvm+1n​−vm−1n​​=0

Rearranging and writing λ=k/h {\lambda=k/h}λ=k/h, we get

vmn+1=1−aλ2vm+1n+1+aλ2vm−1n.\displaystyle v_{m}^{n+1}=\frac{1-a\lambda}{2}v_{m+1}^{n}+\frac{1+a\lambda}{2}v_{m-1}^{n}.vmn+1​=21−aλ​vm+1n​+21+aλ​vm−1n​.

If ∣aλ∣<1 {|a\lambda|<1}∣aλ∣<1 (so that the scheme is stable, as an important criterion we will note later), we see that the two coefficients on the RHS are positive, and sum up to 1 {1}1. This says that as the time level increase, the grid values are somewhat more avaraged, and in particular the maximum (or minimum) cannot increase (or decrease) with time. Such is called a monotone scheme, and we will see that it has a great limitation: it cannot be very accurate. We shall pay attention to two historically important schemes. The first one is
Lax-Wendroff:

vmn+1−vmnk+avm+1n−vm−1n2h−a2k2⋅vm+1n−2vmn+vm−1nh2=0\displaystyle \frac{v_{m}^{n+1}-v_{m}^{n}}{k}+a\frac{v_{m+1}^{n}-v_{m-1}^{n}}{2h}-\frac{a^{2}k}{2}\cdot\frac{v_{m+1}^{n}-2v_{m}^{n}+v_{m-1}^{n}}{h^{2}}=0kvmn+1​−vmn​​+a2hvm+1n​−vm−1n​​−2a2k​⋅h2vm+1n​−2vmn​+vm−1n​​=0

Apparently higher order derivative approximations are included, and as a result we get a higher order of accuracy. One can also show that the scheme is stable if and only if ∣aλ∣<1 {|a\lambda|<1}∣aλ∣<1. More importantly, this scheme is dissipative, meaning that the higher frequency part is always dampened more than the lower frequency part. The second one is
Crank-Nicolson:

vmn+1−vmnk+avm+1n+1−vm−1n+1+vm+1n−vm−1n4h=0\displaystyle \frac{v_{m}^{n+1}-v_{m}^{n}}{k}+a\frac{v_{m+1}^{n+1}-v_{m-1}^{n+1}+v_{m+1}^{n}-v_{m-1}^{n}}{4h}=0kvmn+1​−vmn​​+a4hvm+1n+1​−vm−1n+1​+vm+1n​−vm−1n​​=0

We find that both vmn+1 {v_{m}^{n+1}}vmn+1​ and vm+1n+1 {v_{m+1}^{n+1}}vm+1n+1​ are included, so that the values at the next time level cannot be immeidately obtained. Such is called an implicit scheme. To solve for such a sheme, considering all grid points in the two time levels and grouping them on both sides, we find that

(⋱⋱⋱a4h1k−a4h⋱⋱⋱)(⋮vm−1n+1vmn+1vm+1n+1⋮)=(⋮a4hvm−1n+1kvmn−a4hvm+1n⋮),\displaystyle \begin{pmatrix}\\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots\\ & & \frac{a}{4h} & \frac{1}{k} & -\frac{a}{4h}\\ & & & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots\\ \\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\vdots\\ v_{m-1}^{n+1}\\ v_{m}^{n+1}\\ v_{m+1}^{n+1}\\ \vdots \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\vdots\\ \\ \frac{a}{4h}v_{m-1}^{n}+\frac{1}{k}v_{m}^{n}-\frac{a}{4h}v_{m+1}^{n}\\ \\ \vdots \end{pmatrix},​​⋱​⋱4ha​​⋱k1​⋱​−4ha​⋱​⋱​​​⋮vm−1n+1​vmn+1​vm+1n+1​⋮​​=​⋮4ha​vm−1n​+k1​vmn​−4ha​vm+1n​⋮​​,

which amounts to solving a tridiagonal system. We won't discuss much about how to solve this, but note that it is one of the reasons that Crank-Nicolson is appealing. We shall focus on the stability property of the scheme: in contrast to the previous explicit schemes, Crank-Nicolson scheme is unconditionally stable. In fact, as a corollary of Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy condition, there are NO explicit, unconditionally stable, consistent finite difference schemes for hyperbolic system of PDEs. {\quad}

Now one can already see a large variety of finite difference schemes that at first look are all somewhat plausible for computing the approximate solution. So the job to analyse these schemes, even in the simple case of one way wave equation, is not trivial and can be difficult and cumbersome even with the right tools. Nevertheless, the general problem correspond to the linear PDE Pu=f {Pu=f}Pu=f is of the form

Pk,hv=Rk,hf\displaystyle P_{k,h}v=R_{k,h}fPk,h​v=Rk,h​f

where Pk,h {P_{k,h}}Pk,h​ is a finite difference operator and Rk,h {R_{k,h}}Rk,h​ is an approximation of the identity operator. The assesment of the finite difference operator will be based on several notions that we will introduce later. Before that, we need the machinary of Fourier transform.

1.3. A quick review of L2 {L^{2}}L2 theory of Fourier series

At a certain time level, the function vm {v_{m}}vm​ is defined on the spatial gird which is isomorphic to hZ {h\mathbb{Z}}hZ. We will consider the grid functions that are squared summable: vm∈ℓ2(hZ) {v_{m}\in\ell^{2}(h\mathbb{Z})}vm​∈ℓ2(hZ). Applying the Fourier transform to vm {v_{m}}vm​, we get

v^(ξ)=∑m=−∞+∞vmh⋅e−imhξ(3) \displaystyle \hat{v}(\xi)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{+\infty}v_{m}h\cdot e^{-imh\xi} (3)v^(ξ)=m=−∞∑+∞​vm​h⋅e−imhξ(3)

for ξ∈[−π/h,π/h] {\xi\in[-\pi/h,\pi/h]}ξ∈[−π/h,π/h], which can be easily checked to be a function lying in L2[−πh,πh] {L^{2}[-\frac{\pi}{h},\frac{\pi}{h}]}L2[−hπ​,hπ​]. Parseval's identity asserts that Fourier transform is a unitary transform from ℓ2(hZ) {\ell^{2}(h\mathbb{Z})}ℓ2(hZ) to L2[−πh,πh] {L^{2}[-\frac{\pi}{h},\frac{\pi}{h}]}L2[−hπ​,hπ​], namely the norms are preserved

∥v∥h2=h∑m=−∞+∞∣vm∣2=∫−πhπh∣v^(ξ)∣2dξ=∥v^∥2.\displaystyle \|v\|_{h}^{2}=h\sum_{m=-\infty}^{+\infty}|v_{m}|^{2}=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{h}}^{\frac{\pi}{h}}|\hat{v}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi=\|\hat{v}\|^{2}.∥v∥h2​=hm=−∞∑+∞​∣vm​∣2=∫−hπ​hπ​​∣v^(ξ)∣2dξ=∥v^∥2.

And the Fourier inversion formula

vm=12π∫−πhπheimhξv^(ξ)dξ(4) \displaystyle v_{m}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\frac{\pi}{h}}^{\frac{\pi}{h}}e^{imh\xi}\hat{v}(\xi)d\xi (4)vm​=2π​1​∫−hπ​hπ​​eimhξv^(ξ)dξ(4)

that recovers the grid function from its Fourier transform. So Fourier transform from ℓ2(hZ) {\ell^{2}(h\mathbb{Z})}ℓ2(hZ) to L2[−πh,πh] {L^{2}[-\frac{\pi}{h},\frac{\pi}{h}]}L2[−hπ​,hπ​] is in fact an isometry. Because of the above facts, we will in turn study the Fourier transform v^(ξ) {\hat{v}(\xi)}v^(ξ) of the grid function at certain time level, and how it evolutes with time.

The first observation to make is that, by (4), vm {v_{m}}vm​ is now a superposition of waves of frequencies ξ∈[−π/h,π/h] {\xi\in[-\pi/h,\pi/h]}ξ∈[−π/h,π/h], with ampflitude v^(ξ) {\hat{v}(\xi)}v^(ξ). The high frequecy component correspond to the more oscillating behavior of the grid function. Thus if the computed solution vm {v_{m}}vm​ is non-smooth or oscillating quickly, we would expect a large value of v^(ξ) {\hat{v}(\xi)}v^(ξ) for ∣ξ∣ {|\xi|}∣ξ∣ large. This corresponds to the fact that the more non-smooth the function get, the slower the decay of its Fourier transform.

Another notable fact is that Fourier transform turns ``differentiation'' into ``multiplication''. This also has a (though not perfect) analog in the discrete case (as differentiation is not available). Indeed, differencing (4) under the integral sign, we see that for example vm+1−vmh=12π∫−πhπh1h(ei(m+1)hξ−eimhξ)v^(ξ)dξ=12π∫−πhπh(eihξ−1h)eimhξv^(ξ)dξ\frac{v_{m+1}-v_{m}}{h} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\frac{\pi}{h}}^{\frac{\pi}{h}}\frac{1}{h}(e^{i(m+1)h\xi}-e^{imh\xi})\hat{v}(\xi)d\xi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\frac{\pi}{h}}^{\frac{\pi}{h}}\left(\frac{e^{ih\xi}-1}{h}\right)e^{imh\xi}\hat{v}(\xi)d\xihvm+1​−vm​​=2π​1​∫−hπ​hπ​​h1​(ei(m+1)hξ−eimhξ)v^(ξ)dξ=2π​1​∫−hπ​hπ​​(heihξ−1​)eimhξv^(ξ)dξ. By this we will be able to obtain certain recurrence relation for the Fourier transfrom v^n(ξ) {\hat{v}^{n}(\xi)}v^n(ξ) for different time levels. This is the basis of von Neumann analysis.

1.4. Convergence; accuracy and stability

Now we are ready to formalize notion of a ``good'' finite difference scheme. Because the solution of a PDE need not be differentiable in general, the following is formulated in terms of test functions.

Definition 1 (Consistency and accuracy) A finite difference scheme Pk,hv=Rk,hf {P_{k,h}v=R_{k,h}f}Pk,h​v=Rk,h​f is said to be consistent with the PDE Pu=f {Pu=f}Pu=f if for any smooth function ϕ {\phi}ϕ

Pk,hϕ−Rk,h(Pϕ)=o(1)\displaystyle P_{k,h}\phi-R_{k,h}\left(P\phi\right)=o(1)Pk,h​ϕ−Rk,h​(Pϕ)=o(1)

where o(1) {o(1)}o(1) is a quantity that goes to zero as k,h→0 {k,h\rightarrow0}k,h→0. The scheme is said to be accurate of order (p,q) {(p,q)}(p,q) if

Pk,hϕ−Rk,h(Pϕ)=O(kp+hq).\displaystyle P_{k,h}\phi-R_{k,h}\left(P\phi\right)=O(k^{p}+h^{q}).Pk,h​ϕ−Rk,h​(Pϕ)=O(kp+hq).

Definition 2 (Stability for first order homogeneous equations) A finite difference scheme Pk,hv=0 {P_{k,h}v=0}Pk,h​v=0 for a first order PDE is said to be stable in the stability region Λ {\Lambda}Λ if for every k,h∈Λ {k,h\in\Lambda}k,h∈Λ, the ℓ2 {\ell^{2}}ℓ2 norm of the grid function at time level n {n}n is basically bounded by, or perhaps sums of, the ℓ2 {\ell^{2}}ℓ2 norms of the gird functions at initial times, i.e. there is an integer J>0 {J>0}J>0 and constant CT {C_{T}}CT​

∥vn∥h≤CT∑j=0J∥vj∥h.\displaystyle \|v^{n}\|_{h}\leq C_{T}\sum_{j=0}^{J}\|v^{j}\|_{h}.∥vn∥h​≤CT​j=0∑J​∥vj∥h​.

The idea of stability of a scheme is that only reasonable amount of growth of the computed solution is allowed.

Finally we define convergence, which is slightly more involved, since we have to specify in what sense the discrete solution vmn {v_{m}^{n}}vmn​ should converges to the true solution u {u}u as the grid becomes finer and finer. We shall define the convergence in L2 {L^{2}}L2, but vmn {v_{m}^{n}}vmn​ lies essentially on a different space than u {u}u. To remedy, we interpolate the vmn {v_{m}^{n}}vmn​'s to get a function defined on the domain of u {u}u, using the Fourier inversion formula. Recall that we have

vm=12π∫−πhπheimhξv^(ξ)dξ.\displaystyle v_{m}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\frac{\pi}{h}}^{\frac{\pi}{h}}e^{imh\xi}\hat{v}(\xi)d\xi.vm​=2π​1​∫−hπ​hπ​​eimhξv^(ξ)dξ.

Embbeding hZ {h\mathbb{Z}}hZ into R {\mathbb{R}}R, we define

Sv(x)=12π∫−πhπheixξv^(ξ)dξ,\displaystyle \mathcal{S}v(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\frac{\pi}{h}}^{\frac{\pi}{h}}e^{ix\xi}\hat{v}(\xi)d\xi,Sv(x)=2π​1​∫−hπ​hπ​​eixξv^(ξ)dξ,

where S {\mathcal{S}}S is called the cardinal spline operator. It's easy to see that the Fourier transform of Sv(x) {\mathcal{S}v(x)}Sv(x) is such that

Sv^(ξ)={v^(ξ)∣ξ∣≤π/h0otherwise.\displaystyle \widehat{\mathcal{S}v}(\xi)=\begin{cases} \hat{v}(\xi) & |\xi|\leq\pi/h\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}.Sv(ξ)={v^(ξ)0​∣ξ∣≤π/hotherwise​.

Definition 3 (Convergence for homogeneous initial value problem) A finite difference scheme approximating the initial value problem of a homogeneous equation is said to be convergent if Svn {\mathcal{S}v^{n}}Svn converges to u(tn,⋅) {u(t_{n},\cdot)}u(tn​,⋅) in L2 {L^{2}}L2, where tn=nk {t_{n}=nk}tn​=nk, for every solution u {u}u to the initial value problem, and for every set of solutions to the differential scheme v {v}v, depending on h {h}h and k {k}k, for which Sv0 {\mathcal{S}v^{0}}Sv0 converges to u(0,⋅) {u(0,\cdot)}u(0,⋅) in L2 {L^{2}}L2 and h,k→0 {h,k\rightarrow0}h,k→0 in the stability region.

Luckily, we don't always need use the definition of convergence to show it, thanks to the following important theorem of Lax and Richtmeyer. So much of the analysis of a scheme reduces to the analysis of its consistency and stability.

Theorem 4 (Lax-Richtmeyer equivalence theorem) A consistent finite difference scheme for a well-posed initial value problem for a PDE is convergent if and only if it is stable.

We next begin stability and accuracy analysis.

1.5. Von Neumann analysis

We first illustrate the method with Forward-time Central-space scheme
